# Keep the Maternal Mortality Task Force. Then Act on It.

Extending the task force is the wrong place to stop. A review panel can tell Texas why mothers are dying, but a diagnosis is not a cure, and the cure belongs to the Legislature. Lawmakers are heading into a special session, and they should renew the task force quickly, without drama or delay. Then they should use the same session to act on what it has already told them. Keeping the panel alive is the easy part. The harder part is doing something with what it finds.

## Why the review matters

The task force's core value is that it reviews deaths one case at a time. That matters because a death label hides what actually happened. A record that names a single cause of death says nothing about the missed appointment, the untreated condition, or the coverage that ran out. Case-by-case review brings those things into view, and they are the places where a policy can intervene.

Critics point to errors in the data, and they are right that errors exist. But the answer to imperfect data is better data, not no review at all. Flawed numbers are a reason to look more closely at individual cases, not to stop looking.

If the task force lapses, the cost is high and hard to undo. Case files go unreviewed, patterns go unseen, and an institution that took years to build has to be assembled again from scratch. Letting the panel lapse would mean Texas stops learning why its mothers die.

## Who dies

Start with the ratio: the gap in death rates between groups of Texas mothers is not a rounding error. The tempting explanation is class, and it does not close that gap. The causes are familiar and often treatable. Untreated hypertension is one, the kind of condition case review turns up behind a death label that names something else. Overdose is another.

## The 60-day cliff

Medicaid pays for roughly half of the births in Texas. That coverage comes with a cliff. Sixty days after delivery, it ends.

The task force's key finding is that deaths cluster after that window closes. Overdose is the clearest postpartum example. A mother who gets treatment during pregnancy often loses it once the baby arrives, because the coverage that paid for it was tied to the pregnancy. Treatment stops just as the risks of the postpartum months continue.

Texas makes this worse than most states. It has not expanded Medicaid, and its eligibility limits are strict. A woman who loses pregnancy coverage at 60 days has few places to turn. She is likely to fall straight into the ranks of the uninsured, with no way to pay for the care she still needs.

The consequence is that mothers die in the months when the state has stopped paying attention. Of everything the task force could recommend, one fix deserves the most pressure: extend postpartum coverage to 12 months. It is the direct answer to the finding. If deaths cluster after the 60-day window, the window is what needs to change. Twelve months of coverage would keep treatment going for the women who now lose it, including those with hypertension and those in recovery from addiction.

## The real test

Renewing the task force is an easy vote. Nobody will campaign against studying maternal deaths, and a unanimous show of support costs lawmakers nothing. The hard test comes after that vote, when the findings call for spending money and changing the rules.

The task force has done its part. It has named the problem and shown where the deaths fall. The question for this session is whether the Legislature will do its part.

Reformers who want to reduce the number of women dying during and after childbirth scored an important victory recently. The Legislature approved funding to keep the Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force going.

That's great. But the task force is an extension of an existing government commission, the Quality Improvement Commission. And while the task force has had success, that's not the main reason Gov. Greg Abbott and legislative leaders should have extended its life.

The task force, for the most part, just collects information. Its work is valuable, and it deserves the support of everyone who cares about women's health.

The task force collects data on maternal deaths, and it analyzes those deaths to see what caused them. But the ultimate goal isn't just to gather information. The task force's work is supposed to lead to changes that lower the state's maternal mortality rate, which is higher than the national rate and ranks near the bottom among states.

The Legislature and the governor should already be trying to lower the state's maternal mortality rate. That's what the Legislature and governor are elected to do.

The Legislature isn't just a data-gathering body. It's a policymaking body.

The task force's work is important. But even its final report this year didn't try to directly address the root causes of maternal mortality. It didn't, for example, propose that the state expand Medicaid coverage to pregnant women or that it give women more flexibility in accessing health care after their babies are born.

The task force is trying to figure out how to reduce maternal mortality. But the Legislature shouldn't be waiting for a task force to give them the answers. Policymakers should be doing what they were elected to do: Make the tough choices that will help women stay safe during and after their pregnancies.

The Legislature could fund paid family leave, and it could expand Medicaid coverage to pregnant women and their newborns. It could make certain that more women get their pregnancies on track by ensuring they get the care they need when they need it. And it could ensure that more women have time off from work after giving birth.

The task force is important. But the Legislature shouldn't leave all the policymaking up to a government commission. The Legislature should be making the hard choices itself.

The problem with the Maternal Mortality Task Force, despite good work on its behalf by the Texas Legislature, is that it hasn't done anything yet. It's just beginning to diagnose what's wrong with Texas' maternal health system, which has the country's fourth highest rate of maternal death. Until it issues its report and the Legislature responds, this task force is a study in motion. Completing the task is the Legislature's job. Acting on it is the Legislature's job, too, and that requires calling a special session. Until the task force completes its work, though, it won't have recommendations that the Legislature can adopt. So let's not put the brakes on anything until the task force's report is out.

## Why the review matters

The best way to make sure that the maternal death diagnosis is right is to review each case. When a woman dies during or shortly after pregnancy, the state already does this, but only in a small number of cases. In Texas, a woman has to die for seven days after birth, for example, for the review to apply. The task force wants to extend that review to cover at least 50 percent of all maternal deaths - that's about 13 deaths a year. The point is, if you don't review each death, you might miss something. And that's what a case in Texas showed. A case with a complicated medical background, but with one detail that a review might have caught. And a detail that has made some lawmakers question whether the state's maternal mortality rate is as high as the data show.

## Who dies

The task force's report says that between 2010 and 2013, 1 in 6 of the women who died were Black, but that Black women make up just 12 percent of the state's population. It also says that Black women are three times more likely to die from maternal health complications than other women. The task force says that a major cause is untreated hypertension, which often goes untested or untreated in pregnant women, but which can be very dangerous during pregnancy. In the case that's at the center of this review, the task force says that the woman had high blood pressure, but she had not received medical care that would have identified it. That's the point of the review. If it had happened, it might have saved her life.

## The 60-day cliff

The Task Force's report says that most maternal deaths happen between 60 days before a birth and 60 days after one - what it calls "the maternal mortality cliff". And it says that many of those deaths happen in Texas, where Medicaid covers more than half of all births. About half of the women who die of maternal complications are covered by Medicaid. And Texas has rejected the Medicaid expansion, which would have extended coverage to more women and cut down on the number of uninsured women. As a result, Medicaid isn't available to more than half of women who would be eligible for it under the expansion. The Task Force's report says that deaths happen on both sides of that cliff, with the majority of them after birth and in the postpartum period - the first 12 months after a baby is born. That's when the state stops paying for medical treatment, and because of that, women don't get the care that they need.

## The real test

There are lawmakers who say that the Task Force has already done enough. They want to keep it and make sure that it continues to do its work. They're right, but that's not the hard part. The hard part will come when the report is out and the Legislature has to decide what to do about it. There are lawmakers who are worried that the Task Force will propose policies that are too extreme, or that it won't be able to agree on what to do. And there are lawmakers who say that the Task Force doesn't do enough, that the report is just a way to "study the problem to death". Those lawmakers are wrong. For starters, the Task Force isn't a policymaking body; it just makes recommendations. But the real test will come when the Task Force has made its recommendations and the Legislature has to decide what to do about it. That's the hard part. That's when the Task Force will have to make the case for the policies that it's recommending, and the state lawmakers will have to decide whether they want to adopt them.

# Seven Words: What Can Only Be Said

[Gibran's provocation, quoted in one line.]

Here is the rule this piece rests on: some things exist only when they are said. No act can stand in for them. A gesture can accompany them, support them, even make them believable, but it cannot be them. The saying is the thing itself.

Action is eloquent, and I won't pretend otherwise. A hand on a shoulder, a meal cooked, a door held open: these speak, and sometimes they speak better than sentences do. But eloquence is not the same as precision, and the words below are about precision. They are the ones where the doing falls short.

Look at the list I ended up with, and notice what is missing. Nothing on it is pointable. You cannot gesture at any of these words and say, "There, that one." Every item on the list is something you can only hear, say, or take on trust. I didn't plan that. It was what remained once I removed everything an action could do.

## Love

This is the strongest case for the rule, because the acts that seem to carry love are so often ambiguous. Someone drives across town for you. Is that love, duty, habit, guilt? Someone remembers how you take your coffee. Is that devotion, or just good memory? The act alone cannot say.

Saying it is a risk. That is part of why we avoid it. Implication is comfortable: it lets us mean something without owning it, and it lets the other person decline to notice. Said aloud, the word leaves no room to hide. It can be heard and answered, and it can be refused. That exposure is exactly what makes it count.

None of this makes the acts worthless. The drive, the coffee, the quiet attention are all real. But on their own they are evidence waiting for a verdict. The word is the verdict. Once it is spoken, every earlier act is reread in its light, and what was ambiguous becomes unmistakable. The word gives the acts their meaning.

## Forgive

The sharpest line in this draft is also the simplest: you cannot forgive someone by doing something.

Apology can be mimed. A bowed head, a bunch of flowers, a long and awkward silence at the door: these can all say sorry without a syllable. Forgiveness has no such stand-in. Staying in the room is not forgiveness. Resuming normal life is not forgiveness. Those can be tolerance, exhaustion, or avoidance, and the person who wronged you has no way of telling which.

Spoken, the word does something an act cannot. It releases both parties. The one who was wronged puts down the claim they have been holding. The one who did the wronging is told, plainly, that the claim is gone. Neither has to guess, and neither has to keep carrying it.

A hug after a quarrel is ambiguous. It might mean everything is settled, or it might mean nobody wants to talk. The words are not ambiguous. This echoes what we saw with love: the act leaves a question open, and the word closes it.

## Friend, Believe

These two belong together. Both are words that change a relationship, or hand something over, simply by being spoken.

Take "friend." Saying it is a kind of promotion. Two people can spend years in each other's company, sharing jokes and favors, and still be something undefined. Then one of them says the word, and the relationship is no longer the same. Naming changes the thing. [Personal anecdote about the first time someone was called a friend, to be supplied.]

"Believe" works the same way, and it works because it is spoken aloud. Believing someone silently is private and invisible; they cannot lean on it. Said out loud, it becomes something you give them. It is a transfer of trust, made at the moment of speaking, and the listener can hold it from then on.

[One personal line about being told "I believe you," to be supplied.]

In both cases, the word is not a report on something that already happened. It is the event.

## Always

This is where the argument ends. Actions are trapped in the present. Whatever you do, you do now. You can hold someone's hand today, show up this week, keep a promise this year, but each of those is a single moment, and none of them reaches past itself.

Only words reach forward. "Always" is a claim about a time that has not arrived, and an act has no grammar for that. A gesture cannot say "and tomorrow, too." Only the word can stretch the present into a future and bind the speaker to it.

That is also why it is the riskiest word on the list. To say "always" is to promise something you cannot yet know you can deliver. Time will test it, and it may fail the test. The speaker has no guarantee, only the willingness to say it anyway and to be held to it.

Every other word here asks you to be brave in the moment. This one asks you to be brave for as long as you have said you will be.

Gibran once said that words are the cask wherein wine of wisdom is poured and offered to neighbors, not the wine itself. It's a bold statement, but also one which neatly illustrates the importance of what we say, and how we say it. Nothing worth saying can ever be said perfectly, but everything worth saying can be ruined by its mere attempt. The same is true of fiction writing, which is why understanding the power of implication is essential to creating narratives that are as compelling and memorable as possible.

The golden rule to understanding the power of implication, is to avoid saying anything which can be conveyed simply and effectively through actions. That's not to say that spoken lines shouldn't be used at all, but it does mean that one should be wary of using them to convey things that can be conveyed through action. Let's look at the example of love, which is perhaps the most basic, and arguably the most important emotion of all. Saying the words 'I love you' is an easy and powerful sentence, but one which is equally open to misinterpretation as it is to meaning. Actions are much more clear, and they can be much more eloquent in conveying the nature of a character's love than any spoken words.

The power of implication doesn't only apply to positive emotions, it also applies to negative ones, and this can be demonstrated by the example of forgiveness. There's no shortage of films and television shows featuring characters delivering heart-rending apologies to their friends, family and loved ones. However, while these apologies can be deeply moving, they rarely match the raw power of an act of forgiveness which is purely wordless. Two characters hugging each other in the wake of a bitter argument need say nothing to their audience to make them understand the true meaning of their forgiveness.

Another powerful example of the power of implication is provided by the words 'friend' and 'believe'. By applying these terms to someone, we are effectively elevating them to a new level of importance in our lives, and often giving them more power than we had initially intended. However, there's no need to say these words to a character to convey their importance, merely having them perform an act which reveals this is often all that's required to convey the importance of the relationship. The flipside to the word 'believe' is perhaps even more compelling, because it can mean the difference between life and death. When a character says that they believe in someone, they are giving that person a reason to live, and to fight, even when all hope seems lost.

While the power of implication can be applied to broad and abstract concepts like the ones described above, it can also be applied to much simpler ones, and it is here where we find the most compelling examples of all. The reason that implication is so powerful, is because it allows you to present a situation and its consequences in such a way that the audience's mind fills in the gaps for you. When you do this, you are giving the audience a much greater sense of ownership over the story than you would be if you provided them with everything. It also allows you to draw attention to the things you want your audience to notice, and in doing so, you provide them with the opportunity to interpret your creation in a way that feels more personal and satisfying than an explicit telling would.

# Body Language as the Silent Driver of Conversation

You have probably heard that 93 percent of communication is nonverbal. It is one of the most repeated claims in the field, and it is wrong. It comes from Albert Mehrabian's research, which was narrow: it looked at how people judge feelings and attitudes when words and tone of voice or facial expression disagree. It never said that 93 percent of all meaning lives outside the words.

So drop the number. But keep the line that body language matters, because the real finding points at something useful. When what we say and how we say it pull in different directions, listeners trust the how. Body language is not most of the message. It is the silent driver of how the message lands, and of how the conversation feels.

## Two channels

Every conversation runs on two channels at once. One carries content: the facts, the request, the argument. The other carries the relationship: whether you respect the person, whether you are at ease, whether you are with them or against them. Words do most of the work on the first channel. Body language does a great deal on the second, and the second sets the frame for everything that follows.

Consider a mismatch. You tell a colleague, "Sure, I'd love to hear your idea," while glancing at your phone with your arms crossed. The content says yes. The relationship channel says you'd rather be elsewhere, and that is the message they will believe.

Now the mirror. You say the same words, put the phone down, turn toward them and lean in slightly. The channels agree, and the invitation is real.

## Alignment, not performance

The core principle is alignment. Your body should say what you actually mean, not what you wish you meant. This is the strongest idea in the whole subject, and it changes how to think about technique.

Faking fails because incongruence gets detected. A practiced smile over irritation, a staged nod over boredom, an open posture held over resentment: people may not name what is wrong, but they sense the gap between signal and intent, and they trust you less for it. Performance adds a second layer of mismatch on top of the first.

The legitimate kind of adjustment is removing noise. Much of what bodies do is not intent at all: the fidgeting, the glance at the clock, the clenched jaw, the arms folded only because the room is cold. Clearing that away lets your real intent come through undistorted. You are not adding a signal. You are clearing the static.

The limit case follows directly. If you don't mean it, no posture will say it for you. Fix the intent first, or accept that the body will report the truth.

## Where it counts: hard conversations

Hard conversations are where body language does the most work, and the first risk is the least obvious: unintended dominance. Standing while the other person sits, leaning over a desk, or speaking from behind a barrier can make you loom even when your words are gentle. The person hears a threat you never meant to send.

The fix is concrete. Match their level. Sit if they are sitting, angle your chair rather than facing them squarely across a table, and remove the obstacle between you.

Counterintuitively, less eye contact can help with difficult topics. Steady, unbroken eye contact on a painful subject can feel like an interrogation. Looking away at natural moments, at a notepad or the middle distance, gives the other person room to think and to feel without being watched.

Watch your gestures too. Pointing, chopping hands, and sharp jabbing motions escalate tension, because they read as pressure even when the words are calm. Keep your hands open and low.

And authority? It comes from stillness, not from taking up space.

## Calibrate both ways

No rule substitutes for watching the person in front of you. Read their response: if they lean back, go quiet or tighten up, something you are doing is landing badly, whatever the advice says. Adjust, and watch again. Norms vary across cultures, so hold any rule loosely.

Calibration also points inward. Your own body is a signal to yourself. Clenched hands or a held breath can tell you what you are feeling before you have admitted it. Notice it, and ask whether your body and your intent agree. That, in the end, is the whole point: alignment.

The tip on body language comes at the end, a scant paragraph, one that rattled under the gaze of a discerning colleague. “You’re missing the point,” she said. “You’re telling people to fake it, to pretend to be something they’re not. That won’t work.”

She was right. She was also spot-on with her follow-up. “The issue,” she added, “isn’t faking it—it’s alignment.”

That brings us to a myth, one that gets trotted out in the introduction. The claim—Mehrabian’s narrow finding, not the gross 93% oversell—is that most of the meaning comes not from what you say but from how you say it. Once we puncture that fast, we can keep the line for the rest of the piece.

To be clear, we’re only doing one thing here: we’re re-drawing the frame. From here on, everything is about content vs. relationship. We’re not going to elaborate on that split further. Instead, we’re going to illustrate it, one example after another.

The first: a mismatch. In the negative end of the spectrum, you could have a content mismatch. Your words talk about the big picture, but your body language makes the topic seem small. Or you could have a more direct mismatch: your words are about the big picture, but your body language is hard to read. Whatever the specifics, you’re giving off mixed signals, and that’s a problem.

And what’s the solution? We’ve got to align ourselves. The conversation is a joint effort, and both parties need to dial into that.

The point here is that the content mismatch is like a noisy signal. It’s the opposite of alignment. The other party can’t hear what you’re saying, and if you want to fix that, you’ve got to remove the noise. There’s nothing wrong with adjusting your body language, but you’ve got to be doing it for the right reason. If you’re feeling relaxed and you push your body language to a more tense state, that’s not an adjustment—that’s a performance. And people will see through it.

So we want to cut the noise. The way to do that is to dial into your intent. In conversations, the more clear your intent, the more aligned your body language will be to it.

The key here is that the intent doesn’t have to be obvious. If your intent is to go to war, you’re going to have a pretty big mismatch with your body language. But that’s the opposite of alignment. Instead, take a look at your most recent hard conversation. Were you trying to lead, or were you trying to avoid? Did your body language reflect that intent?

Let’s bring in an example here, one that’s got both kinds of mismatch: the content mismatch and the relationship mismatch.

2. Where it counts: hard conversations.

# GDP Measures Output, Not Well-Being

Gross domestic product tells us how much an economy produces. It was never built to tell us how well people live, and treating it as if it did produces errors that are easy to make and hard to see. Output can rise while most households gain nothing. It can be large in a country where each person has little. It can leave out work that sustains whole societies, and it can count destruction as progress. Each of these is a gap between what GDP records and what well-being requires, and each deserves a closer look.

## Divide by people first

Total output says little about individual lives until it is divided by the number of people who share it. Consider two countries. Country A produces four times as much as Country B, yet its output per head is one fifth as large. Ranking by total output puts A far ahead. Ranking by output per head reverses the order, and the second ranking is the one closer to ordinary living standards.

The sharpest consequence concerns growth. An economy can post rising GDP while its people grow worse off. If population increases faster than output, the total climbs and output per head falls. Headline growth then masks decline. The figure that gets reported and celebrated moves up while the average person's share moves down. A reader who sees a growth rate without the population trend behind it can be misled about the direction of change, not merely its size. This is why per capita figures should be the default, and why a total deserves suspicion when it appears alone.

Comparisons across countries should also adjust for purchasing power parity, which corrects for the different price levels in each place, since the same income buys different amounts in different countries.

## Averages hide who gets it

Even output per head describes a mean, and a mean says nothing about distribution. Two countries can have identical output per head and offer their citizens very different lives. Picture one where gains are spread widely and a typical family shares in them. Picture another where a small group captures most of the output, so a typical family has far less than the average suggests. The statistic is the same, but the lives are not.

The bite comes when growth is set against the median. GDP per capita can rise year after year while the income of the median person stays flat or falls, because the gains go to people already above it. The average improves, and the person in the middle sees nothing. Growth reported as a national success then describes the experience of a minority. Judging whether growth reaches ordinary households requires a measure of the middle and the spread, which GDP does not supply.

## Unrecorded work

GDP captures what is traded and measured, so it misses a large amount of productive activity. Work in the informal economy and unpaid work both create value that people depend on, yet neither appears in the accounts. What matters is the consequence, not the categories.

That consequence is a skew in comparisons. A country where much production happens outside recorded markets will look poorer than the work its people actually do would warrant. One where the same tasks are bought and sold will look richer for doing the same things. The distortion falls hardest on developing economies, where more of this activity goes unrecorded. Differences in GDP between countries then partly reflect how much activity gets recorded rather than how much gets done.

## Damage counted as gain

GDP adds up output but never subtracts the costs of producing it. Pollution shows the problem. The activity that generates it adds to output, while the harm it does never enters the ledger as a loss. An economy can degrade its surroundings and report only the gain.

The perverse case is disaster cleanup. Spending to clear debris and rebuild is activity, so it raises GDP, even though the disaster left people poorer. What was destroyed goes unrecorded as a loss, while the spending to repair it is counted as a gain.

The root cause is how the measure is built. GDP is assembled from market transactions. It records what is bought and sold at the price paid. Whatever is not exchanged is invisible, and whatever is exchanged counts as positive, whether it makes people better off or merely restores what they had. The measure has no way to tell spending that creates from spending that repairs.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a key indicator used in measuring the economy’s health. GDP is the monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a specific period of time. However, this measurement does not take into account important factors like leisure, life expectancy, or happiness. GDP is not intended to measure well-being, and it is often misinterpreted as a measure of well-being. The human toll of rising inequality, soaring health care and education costs, and rising unemployment are ignored in the GDP measure. In contrast, the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) tries to take into account factors not measured by GDP, like the negative environmental impacts of economic activity.

GDP per capita tells us little about well-being because it does not take into account the distribution of income and/or wealth in a country. It also fails to take into account inequality within a country, and ignores the value of unpaid work. The GPI, on the other hand, accounts for changes in income distribution within a country and attempts to quantify the value of unpaid work such as housework and volunteering.

There are other important factors that are not included in the GDP measure. These include the costs of natural resource depletion and pollution. These costs are not included in the GDP measure because they are not market transactions. If a company pollutes a river, for example, the cost of cleaning up the pollution is included in the GDP measure, but the costs of the pollution itself are not. The GPI measures these costs and subtracts them from the GDP measure.

The GPI is an imperfect measure, but it is a more comprehensive measure than the GDP. By accounting for factors that are not included in the GDP measure, the GPI gives us a more complete picture of a country’s well-being. While the GDP measure may have been useful in the past, it is clear that we need to move beyond it and develop more comprehensive measures of well-being.

GDP Measures Output, Not Well-Being
A GDP measurement, while useful as an indicator of economic output, fails to gauge the well-being of a nation's citizens.

## Divide by people first

A country with four times the population of another, having four times the output, may have a fifth of the output per person of the less populous country. You can see the point when it is better to divide output by people first, and then compare countries. The sharper point is that a country's growth can mask a decline in well-being, so give this measurement its proper place.

## Averages hide who gets it

The same per capita output may give different lives to people. Let's consider a concrete case where a country's output grows from $20,000 to $30,000 per person per year. This is a 50% increase. However, if we look at median income, that may have decreased, due to a reduction in the middle of the distribution, with an upward movement of the poor and a lot more growth by the wealthy. The bite is that 20% may have been added to the wealth of 2% of the people, but 2% is not the median. The median is 50% of the distribution, so the bite is that the median person has $19,000, at most, while the median person had $20,000 before. In this case, the median person is actually worse off, even though the country's output has grown.

## Unrecorded work

Unrecorded work and unpaid work can skew comparisons, especially for developing economies. The informal economy - cash transactions, ranging from farming to haircuts to laundering money - represents a significant percentage of economic output in developing economies, yet this output is generally not included in national accounts. As well, much of the work that people perform around the world is unpaid, such as raising children, maintaining households, and caring for elderly parents. These efforts represent real costs and should be factored into a proper assessment of well-being.

## Damage counted as gain

Pollution contributes to economic output, while the costs of environmental degradation are never subtracted. One perverse example is that the cleanup of a disaster, whether natural or man-made, will add to a nation's GDP. This perverse accounting stems from the very root of GDP, built as it is from market transactions. Gross domestic product is the total of goods and services bought and sold within a country. It includes all market transactions, regardless of their social utility or environmental impact. Anything that is bought and sold is counted as a benefit, including the arms trade, drugs, and the sale of polluting, global-warming, or genetically engineered products.

# Kelp Pills Can Disrupt the Thyroid They Promise to Help

Kelp supplements are marketed as support for the thyroid. They can also disrupt it. The irony is hard to miss: a product sold to protect a gland can be the thing that throws it off. Kelp reaches consumers as pills and in other supplement forms, and the pills are where the trouble concentrates.

## A narrow safe window

The amount an adult needs is tiny. The recommended ceilings are low, and they differ by jurisdiction, so even the official line on "too much" depends on where you live.

The thyroid has a safety brake that usually works. When intake runs high, the gland tends to protect itself. Sometimes the brake fails, and then excess intake disrupts the gland instead of being absorbed harmlessly.

The harm runs in both directions. Too much of the nutrient can push thyroid function off course one way or the other, so the risk is not limited to a single kind of patient. Some people are more exposed than others, and the brake is least reliable in exactly those people.

The effects can also reach a second person. Newborns can be exposed through the mother, so a supplement one adult takes can affect an infant who never chose it.

## Why supplements are the problem

The number that does the work is the gap between what the body needs and what a supplement can deliver. Need is tiny and ceilings are low, so a single pill can overshoot both. That is the core problem.

Labels do not close the gap, because they are unreliable. What is printed on the bottle may not match what is inside, so a careful reader can still be wrong about the dose.

Concentration and stacking compound the problem. A concentrated product is risky on its own. Add a second supplement, or a few, and the total becomes invisible. No single label shows the sum, and the person swallowing it all may never add it up.

The sharpest point is about who buys these products. Marketing selects for the vulnerable. A product pitched at thyroid trouble reaches people who are already worried about their thyroid, which means it reaches the people least able to absorb a mistake. The audience is not a random cross-section of the public. It is the group the pitch is built to attract, and it is the group with the most to lose if the brake fails. The promise of help is the mechanism that delivers the product to those it can hurt most. The risk is not spread evenly and then occasionally concentrated by bad luck. The sales pitch concentrates it on purpose, or at least by design.

This is not only theory. There is evidence of real harm.

One check is concrete. Look at the label and add up the amount from every supplement you take, not just the kelp. If you cannot find or trust the number, treat that as the answer.

## The Japan objection

The strongest objection comes from Japan. Intake there is far above Western limits, and there is no crisis. If high intake were dangerous, the argument goes, Japan would show it.

The key contrast is adaptation versus sudden start. A population that has eaten a certain way for generations has adapted. Someone who starts a concentrated pill tomorrow has not. The brake may hold for the first and fail for the second.

The comparison also breaks down on the details. Species differ, preparation differs, and day-to-day intake swings. Food is not a pill. Kelp eaten as part of meals, prepared in a particular way, varies from one day to the next, while a pill delivers the same concentrated dose every time. The Japanese diet and the supplement aisle are not the same exposure, even when both involve kelp.

Even Japan has documented cases. A high-intake country with no crisis still has people who were harmed, which shows the window is narrow there too. Adaptation lowers the risk without removing it. The objection, taken seriously, supports the case against the pills rather than undermining it.

The need for iodine is tiny. Adults are advised to get about 150 micrograms a day. For pregnant women, it's 220 micrograms. And for those who breastfeed, the recommended dosage goes up to 290 micrograms. All of this iodine is usually found in the diet, and so a supplement is not necessary. These are upper limits. Excessive amounts of iodine can also be harmful. Too much iodine can disrupt hormone action, and this is why. The thyroid gland produces hormones that regulate how quickly the body burns calories and uses energy. Iodine regulates this function, and there is a safety brake. But this brake sometimes doesn't work.

## Why supplements are the problem

The problem is that when iodine is taken as a supplement, the thyroid gland cannot tell how much iodine is normal and how much is too much. The available iodine is regulated by the pituitary gland, but this organ cannot distinguish between iodine from seaweed pills and iodine already in the diet. So it's easy to take too much. And iodine excess is hard to detect, since you cannot see any signs. In fact, a goiter might form, but this is hard to see. The only effective way to check for an iodine toxicity is to test the blood. Kelp pills are marketed as a thyroid health supplement, but they can disrupt the thyroid.

## The Japan objection

You might object that there is no epidemic of iodine toxicity in Japan, where the consumption of seaweed is at higher levels than in the west. However, this objection doesn't hold up. The Japanese eat seaweed regularly, but they prepare it in different ways. The preparation reduces the iodine content, and this lowers the intake to safe levels. And Japanese consumption fluctuates over time, as traditional foods give way to modern foods. There are documented cases of Japanese iodine poisoning. This can happen suddenly, and if it does, then there is no time to adapt. The sharp contrast is between a gradual adaptation to gradual changes in iodine levels, and the sharp spike of a sudden overdose. This is why seaweed consumption is safe in Japan but not in the west.

# Bubbles: What Makes Some Burst Harder and Heal Slower

A bubble is a stretch in which the price of an asset is driven by what people expect it to fetch later, not by what the asset produces. The mechanism is a self-fulfilling expectation. Buyers expect prices to rise, so they buy, and their buying makes prices rise, which confirms the expectation and draws in more buyers.

The burst comes when the buyers are exhausted. Nobody is left to pay a higher price, and the expectation that held everything up gives way. But the burst itself is not what matters most. What matters is what decides how bad it gets, and that is the question this piece follows.

## Debt turns a crash into a crisis

Leverage is the multiplier. A crash in which people lose only their own savings hurts, but it stays contained. A crash in which people borrowed to buy becomes something worse, because borrowed money has to be repaid whatever the asset is now worth.

The spiral runs in a clear order. Borrowers default. Lenders, now exposed to losses, retreat and stop lending. Those who still hold debt are forced to sell, and their forced selling pushes prices down further, which creates more defaults. Each step feeds the next.

It usually starts with cheap money flowing into assets. Easy borrowing pushes prices up, rising prices make the assets look safe to borrow against, and that invites more borrowing. The boom feeds itself on the way up, and the same loop runs in reverse on the way down.

The 2008 crisis shows the whole chain in a single case. Housing and credit were not two separate stories but one. Cheap money poured into housing, and when housing fell, the losses did not stay there. They moved into the financial institutions that had lent against it. That is contagion: trouble in one market spreading through the balance sheets that connected it to everything else.

Contagion also reaches innocent bystanders. People and businesses that never speculated on housing found credit harder to get once lenders pulled back. A crash that begins among borrowers and lenders ends up costing people who had no part in the bubble.

## Recovery is measured in decades

The dot-com bubble was built on valuations with nothing underneath. Prices reflected hope about what companies might become, not anything the companies were producing. When the buyers ran out, those prices had nothing to rest on, and they fell hard.

The fall was severe, but the more striking number is the time it took to recover. It took fifteen years for the market to get back to where it had been. A whole working career's worth of patience was needed just to break even for those who bought at the top.

Japan is the extreme case, because the bubble was not confined to one sector. It was an entire economy. When everything is priced on expectation, and the debt behind it is large, there is no healthy part left to pull the rest back up.

The number to remember is thirty. Japan's recovery has been counted in thirty years.

That is the real cost of buying late. Early buyers sold into the enthusiasm and took their gains. Late buyers paid the highest prices, on the most extreme expectations, and then waited the longest, in some cases for decades, to see them justified. The burst is a single moment, but the people who bought last carry its cost for a generation.

## What to watch, and the one defense that matters

First, a caveat, stated once: none of this tells you when. Bubbles can run far longer than seems reasonable, and no signal here is a timing tool.

What you can do is run a concrete check instead of relying on a feeling. Look at how much of the buying is financed by borrowing. This ties directly back to the debt section, and it is the sign that predicts severity. A bubble funded by cash is painful. A bubble funded by leverage is the kind that turns into a crisis.

Then apply the dot-com lesson. Ask whether the price has anything underneath it, meaning whether the asset produces something that justifies what people are paying, or whether the price depends only on someone else paying more later.

Then apply a personal test. Ask whether you could hold your position through a fall and a very long recovery without needing the money.

Of all the advice one could give, only the leverage advice is worth keeping, because it mirrors the mechanism that does the damage. Don't borrow to buy something whose price rests on expectation. Debt is what turns a falling price into a deadline.

That is the whole defense: don't be a forced seller. The spiral of default, lender retreat and forced selling runs on people who have no choice but to sell at the bottom. If you are not one of them, the burst can hurt your portfolio without taking your future, and that is the reason to hold the fund the way you do: so that you can wait.

Bubbles are some of the most volatile and most worrisome of financial phenomena. Yet they also capture the human fascination with extremes. It’s easy to see how they draw attention when asset prices rise rapidly and then collapse. It’s harder to understand their spread and severity, but understanding the risk factors can help investors weather them and avoid ruin.

The Bubble is a Uniquely Financial Phenomenon

The first step toward understanding the risks bubbles pose is to define what a bubble is. A bubble is when asset prices rise on the expectation of ever-rising prices, with little regard for underlying fundamentals. Think tulip bulbs in Holland in the 1600s, stocks in the US in the 1920s, tech stocks in the late 1990s, and housing in the mid-2000s. With bubbles, prices become detached from underlying value and reality.

Price is Driven by Expectation, Not Output

The most vivid part of bubbles is their rapid rise and collapse. The rise occurs because investors believe prices will rise, so they bid up asset prices, which in turn reinforces their belief. The fall occurs when this self-fulfilling expectation breaks down, often when the price becomes too high relative to some reference point, such as its historic price, or when the cost of carrying the asset becomes a problem. Because so much of a bubble’s rise is built on expectation, this mechanism can lead to overshooting—meaning prices fall below their intrinsic value. This is why it’s important to understand what drives bubble formation and collapse.

Leverage is the Multiplier

Debt is a crucial element of most bubbles’ formation and spread. Buying assets on margin, when an investor puts down only a fraction of the asset’s price and borrows the rest, increases both potential gains and losses. The more debt, the larger the impact on asset prices and the bigger the losses when prices fall. As debt fueling a bubble builds, some borrowers are forced to sell assets to pay their loans. These forced asset sales can depress prices, triggering more forced selling and further price declines. This is how leverage can act as a multiplier on asset prices—and risks—during a bubble’s formation and collapse.

A bubble’s reach can extend far beyond the asset class with the runaway prices, in part because of the financial system’s interconnectedness. For example, some holders of the asset may have to sell other assets to pay off loans on the bubbly asset, which in turn can depress prices on those other assets. The ensuing losses can trigger margin calls on those other assets, which lead to further forced selling. This is how a bubble can spread beyond its original asset class.

A Bubble Can Turn a Crash Into a Crisis

How much damage a bubble causes depends on how much leverage it fuels, how fast it grows and spreads, and how much the underlying asset is worth. Because these factors differ from bubble to bubble, their outcomes can vary. Some bubbles lead to a crash in the asset class alone, with minimal impact on the broader economy. Others lead to a crisis and broad economic fallout.

A bubble where prices rise rapidly and underlying fundamentals are weak can lead to a crash and panic in the asset class when prices collapse. The ensuing losses can hurt financial firms, which in turn may have to raise cash by selling other assets, which fuels further price declines. If the bubble has spread widely enough, these losses can trigger a full-blown financial crisis. That’s what happened in the US during the subprime housing bubble in the mid-2000s and the ensuing financial crisis. Housing prices were artificially inflated, and the decline in prices devastated asset values. That led to losses and solvency problems for financial firms, which were forced to sell other assets and raise cash. Fears of losses on their loans led lenders to freeze credit, which stifled economic activity and led to a global recession.

Recoveries Are Measured in Decades

Bubbles are unique among financial phenomena because their boom-and-bust cycles are measured in years, while recoveries take much longer. Research into other bubbles suggests that it can take decades to rebuild the wealth lost during bubbles and crashes. Research on the US stock market in the 1920s found that it didn’t regain its 1929 peak until 1954. Similarly, research on the Nikkei Stock Index in Japan found that it didn’t regain its 1989 peak until 2016. That’s not the only downside to bubbles: Some research finds that bubbles and crashes affect economic growth. For example, the collapse of the US housing bubble in the mid-2000s led to the global financial crisis, which in turn led to a deep and prolonged US recession.

What Makes Some Bubbles Worse Than Others

Not all bubbles are alike. The size, speed, and breadth of the bubble are key factors in determining how bad its collapse will be. Bubbles with more leverage will tend to be more severe, as will those that spread to other asset classes and sectors. Bubbles that are built on real fundamentals are less likely to overshoot on the way down, so their collapses are less severe than bubbles with no underlying fundamentals, like tulip bulbs. Bubbles with a contagion mechanism, like subprime mortgages that led to the financial crisis, also tend to be more severe.

The One Factor that Really Matters

The best strategy for dealing with bubbles is to try to avoid being a forced seller. Forced sellers must sell at whatever price they can get, which tends to be near the bottom of the market. Forced sellers don’t care about fundamentals. Instead, they care about avoiding default. That’s why bubbles tend to lead to overshooting, when prices fall below their intrinsic value. Avoiding forced selling means you can wait for asset prices to recover.

Research suggests that there are two good strategies for avoiding becoming a forced seller: hold high-quality assets and don’t overleverage. Some financial firms—particularly those that don’t take on much leverage—can recover from bubbles without government help. Other firms, particularly those that didn’t take on much leverage, need government help to survive. For investors, maintaining a high-quality portfolio and keeping debt low are good ways to avoid being a forced seller during a bubble’s collapse.

# Gaucher Disease's Primed Brain Resists a Virus in Mice

Mice with a form of Gaucher disease that affects the brain fended off Sindbis virus better than expected. The likely reason is that the disease keeps their brains in a standing state of antiviral alert. The same chronic inflammation that usually counts as damage appears, in this test, to have protected them. The findings are preliminary. They come from mice, and nobody yet knows whether they hold for people with the disease or for those who carry a single copy of the faulty gene. The study raises the possibility that the disease's inflammation has a hidden upside.

## An alarm that never switches off

Gaucher disease is genetic. A cell's cleanup system fails, material builds up, and the cells come under strain. Only the neuronopathic forms, those that affect the brain, matter here.

In these forms, the brain shows signs of interferon activity even though no infection is present. The likely explanation is stress. The buildup in the cells appears to drive a chronic alarm that never shuts off, and interferon is the signal that keeps it going. Interferon is a signaling protein that puts cells on guard against viruses.

The usual view is that this kind of inflammation does harm. A brain that is constantly inflamed is generally assumed to be a brain under attack from its own defenses.

The study asked a different question. If the alarm is always on, does it leave the brain better prepared when a real virus arrives?

## The test

The researchers used Sindbis virus to see whether the primed alarm offers any real protection against infection.

The design was simple. Mice modeling neuronopathic Gaucher disease were infected with the virus, and their outcomes were compared with those of healthy mice.

The Gaucher mice resisted the virus better. The authors attribute this to the interferon response that was already running before the infection began.

The result has a bearing on treatment. Suppressing interferon might ease the chronic inflammation, but it would likely come at a cost: it could remove a defense that the brain is actively using.

## The carrier question

Carriers matter because the gene variant behind Gaucher disease is common, and the disease it causes is a real risk. Anything that keeps the variant in circulation is therefore of interest.

One way to explain that is the heterozygote-advantage idea: carrying a single copy of a harmful variant can bring a benefit even though carrying two brings disease. Sickle cell is the standard example.

The authors suggest that something similar may be at work here. Carriers might be better protected against certain viral infections, and that could help explain why the variant persists. They stop short of claiming it. They offer it as a possibility, not a conclusion.

The biggest gap is that the mice in this study modeled full disease, not the carrier state. Carriers have one faulty copy, not two, and there is no evidence that their brains show the same primed alarm. They may show a weaker version of it, or none at all. Until that is tested, the carrier idea rests on an inference from animals with a much more severe condition.

The second gap is that the study used one virus. Primed immunity might not help against others, and it could cut the other way. A brain already on alert might respond to some infections with too much inflammation, and that could cause harm instead of preventing it.

So the open question is whether carriers, with one copy of the variant and no disease, are actually better defended against viruses, or whether the protection seen here exists only in the brains of animals that are sick.

# Marriage Has Always Been Redefined

We are told that marriage is one fixed thing: one man, one woman, passed down unchanged from the beginning, and that any change to it is a break with the past. That story is a myth. Marriage has been defined and redefined by every society that has practiced it, and the version many people call traditional is only one stage in a long sequence of revisions. The question is not whether marriage may change, because it always has. The question is which definition we now live under, and what follows from it.

## Rome: a bargain

In Rome, no priest was required. Consent and intent were enough to make a marriage. The legal core was *affectio maritalis*, the continuing intention of two people to be married to each other. The law did not ask for a ceremony as proof of the bond. It asked whether the couple meant it.

Divorce followed from the same logic. If consent created a marriage, then withdrawn consent could end it. The arrangement held only as long as the intention did.

Love was optional. A marriage could be affectionate, but the law did not require it and did not measure it. Hold onto that detail, because it sets up a later inversion.

The takeaway is simple: in Rome, marriage was a bargain between two consenting parties, not a status conferred by an institution.

## The Church fixes the definition

The next great redefinition came when the Church made marriage a sacrament, a development of the 12th and 13th centuries. The year 1215 is a useful anchor. By then, marriage was no longer simply a matter of private consent. It belonged to the Church.

This is where "one man, one woman, for life" hardens into the form we now call traditional. Consent and intent no longer stood alone as the core of marriage. The union was defined as a sacred and permanent bond, and the definition was fixed accordingly.

It then proved durable. It survived the Reformation, and the states that later emerged inherited it. The definition passed from the Church to the state largely intact, even as the authority behind it changed.

## Love becomes the point

Once the state took over the administration of marriage, the institution began to change again. Marriage became a legal matter, handled by civil authority rather than religious authority.

Then came the inversion of Rome. Romans treated love as optional; we treat it as the point. Marriage is now understood as a union of two people who choose each other because they love each other. Consent still matters, as it did in Rome, but the purpose has been reversed.

This is the pivot of the story, and it explains why the modern question follows. If marriage rests on love and consent between two people, then it is fair to ask why the law should care about anything else.

## Tradition's best case

The best case for tradition begins with caution. Old institutions carry knowledge that is easy to lose, and changing them carelessly can do harm. That caution is reasonable. But history undercuts it here, because the institution being defended has been changed many times.

The strongest substantive claim is procreative: marriage exists to bind together the people who create children and to give those children stability. Stated fairly, it is a serious argument about what marriage is for.

But the answer is direct. We already marry people who cannot have children, or who choose not to, and we do not treat their marriages as lesser. The model we live by rests on consent and commitment, not on procreation.

The religious claim is that marriage belongs to God's design. It deserves one line in reply: the state took over marriage, and civil marriage answers to civil law.

## Where that leaves us

The law attaches real rights and obligations to marriage, so who may marry is not a symbolic question.

Under the model we already live by, which is consent between two people who choose each other, the gender of the couple is irrelevant. It plays no part in what the law asks. Marriage has moved from Roman bargain to sacrament to civil union of love, and at each step it was redefined. The next step does not break with that history. It follows from it.

That’s really the only throat-clearing needed to state the thesis: marriage has always been whatever society defined it to be. From first to last, marriage has been a legal institution, not a religious or philosophical one. Roman law gave us the enduring legal core of affectio maritalis, an agreement between two people to live together as man and wife – the logic of consent followed, in a society that honored few universal principles, from the right to divorce. The motives, or the intention, were legally irrelevant. Marriage wasn’t about love – it was about property, inheritance, legitimacy. Consent was all that mattered, and love was merely optional.
This Roman approach survived the Christianization of Europe, and when the Church eventually defined marriage as one of its seven sacraments, the Roman definition remained intact. The 12th and 13th centuries saw a flourishing of Christian theology, but it’s only in 1215 that we see the Church hardening the definition of marriage, decreeing that all marriages must take place in a church, be performed by a priest, and be witnessed by the community. It was the first step toward establishing marriage as a sacrament. But the Church had to keep its definition of marriage tight, because it was a definition shared by states. The European states inherited it, codified it, and kept it.
Fast-forward through the Reformation, and then the nation-state, and the Church had lost much of its authority over marriage. By the 1700s, the state had taken over the administration of marriage, granting licenses and tracking the legal obligations of marriage, and marriage had become a secular institution with a legal status.
In this context, the modern question of gay marriage follows inexorably. The state’s definition of marriage has always been flexible, always subject to change. The religious argument for marriage had been defeated, and the historic definition had been subject to dramatic revision. The state’s administration of marriage made it a secular institution, subject to the courts and to social change. And the question was no longer about love, but about the secular nature of marriage. The marriage we have now was a product of the state’s administration and the state’s definition, regardless of the procreative arguments that are now being deployed – arguments that we’ve heard before. The state’s administration of marriage has always been the real definition of marriage.

## Rome: a bargain

In fact, women have always had the legal right to marry, because that right could be easily traced back to its origins. Under Roman law, the only requirement for a valid marriage was the "affectio maritalis," which was a mutual consent between a man and a woman to become husband and wife. The presence of a priest, or any witnesses, were not required. Such a marriage had to be consummated, however, so it was valid only if the couple had sex.
Affectio maritalis was the legal core of marriage. Even after the Church made marriage a sacrament around the 5th century, it did not have the power to declare a couple married unless they had the affectio maritalis. If two people wanted to get married, but were afraid to do it publicly, the Church could recognize their marriage in secret if they met the basic requirements. In this way, the Church gained authority over all marriages, even those that happened without its involvement.

## The Church fixes the definition

The Roman church first established marriage as a sacrament in the 12th or 13th century. The church wanted to maintain control over who could get married, and who could get divorced. It was at this time that the church began its relentless attempts to define marriage in terms of "one man, one woman, for life." By 1215, the church hardened its position, requiring that all marriages must have witnesses, which made it much more difficult to have secret marriages.

## Love becomes the point

By the 16th century, after the Protestant Reformation, the church had even less power over marriage. The Roman Church continued to fight against its erosion of control over marriage, but it had been essentially reduced to a sacrament of the state, and not the church. As late as 1603, the church attempted to strengthen its control over marriage with the Council of Iguacu, which declared that "marriage is first and foremost a legal contract, rather than a sacred bond." This decree was in response to the growing secular concept that marriage was about love, and not just property.
In his book, Marriage, AHistory, the historian Lawerencestone makes the point that the church was strongly opposed to the concept of marriage for love, which was thought to weaken the bonds of marriage. But this idea was being promoted by poets and playwrights, who were beginning to challenge the church's complete control of marriage. Shakespeare's play, "AMidsummerNight'sDream," even ends with a marriage driven by love and not arranged by the parents. Of course, love was still not the focus of marriage in the 16th century, but the seeds were being sown for the concept that marriage was more than a legal contract between two families.

Today, proponents of traditional marriage still argue that marriage is "between one man and one woman," and that it is a historical fact. But a cursory glance at the history of marriage shows that marriage has always been an evolving institution. In fact, the only constant in marriage is that it has always been changing.

# Feeling Ready Isn't Being Ready

You open the exam and see a question on a topic you studied. The term looks familiar. You know you've read about it. But when it's time to write the answer, nothing comes. You recognized it, and you couldn't produce it.

The usual explanation is that you didn't study hard enough. That's rarely the real problem. The problem is calibration: your sense of how well you know something doesn't match how well you actually know it.

## Why rereading lies to you

Rereading feels productive because of what it does to the material. The second pass through a chapter is smoother than the first. The words are familiar, the ideas arrive easily, and nothing surprises you. That familiarity produces fluency, and fluency gets mistaken for mastery. You think, "I know this," when what you mean is, "I've seen this before."

Those are different things. Recognition is the ability to know something when it's in front of you. Recall is the ability to produce it with nothing in front of you. Exams test recall. A study method that builds only recognition prepares you for a test nobody is giving.

The research backs this up. In a 2013 review, Dunlosky and colleagues rated common study techniques, and rereading and highlighting came out with low utility. They are popular, and they don't do much for you.

Highlighting has the same flaw. When you highlight a sentence, you've noticed it. You haven't shown that you know it. A page full of yellow is a record of attention, not of learning.

## Test yourself instead

The better alternative is to retrieve what you've learned. In a 2008 study, Karpicke and Roediger found that testing yourself beats rereading for lasting memory.

Self-testing does two jobs at once. It strengthens memory, because pulling something out of your head is itself a form of practice. And it gives you honest feedback, because you either produced the answer or you didn't. That second job is the calibration fix. The feeling of readiness gets replaced by a result.

Say you're studying the causes of World War I. Close the book and try to list them. If you stall after two, you've found the gap early, while there's still time to fix it, rather than discovering it on exam day.

Flashcards, practice questions, or a blank page where you write everything you remember all work. Choose whichever suits the material.

The same logic applies in a classroom. Asking students whether they understand fails for the same reason rereading does: the answer is a feeling, and feelings are unreliable. Production is required. Students have to write, explain, or solve something before anyone knows what they understand.

## Predict, then compare

One practice that builds calibration is the exam wrapper, associated with Marsha Lovett's work at Carnegie Mellon. It's a short exercise attached to a returned exam, designed to get students to look at how they prepared and how it turned out.

The question that matters most is simple: what score did you predict before you took the exam?

Suppose you predicted a 90 and received a 72. That gap is information. It turns a vague feeling into a piece of evidence you can't argue with. You thought you were ready, and the number says otherwise.

Over a semester, the payoff builds. Each prediction and each result teaches you something about your own judgment. You start to learn which kinds of confidence to trust and which to doubt, and your sense of readiness gets closer to the truth.

## The discomfort is the point

Most people avoid self-testing, and the reason is easy to see. It's uncomfortable. Rereading leaves you feeling capable, while a practice test shows you what you don't know.

Bjork's work on desirable difficulties suggests that the discomfort isn't a side effect. The difficulty is the point.

So the rule is this: don't trust the feeling of knowing until you've produced the answer.

I had been studying for hours. I had a list of equations, tricks, insights and techniques to tackle the problems before me. I had read every word of the textbook and highlighted almost everything. I could recall to mind some of the examples from the text. I felt ready to ace the final exam.
As soon as I saw the exam I knew that I was in trouble. All of those equations, tricks, insights and techniques that I spent so much time memorizing, I had no idea how to apply them in real time. They had all come naturally in the example problems. But now, with only minutes to answer all these questions, I couldn't even remember where to begin.
I had studied for hours. I tried my hardest. But I wasn't ready for the exam.
The problem wasn't my effort. It was my calibration. I thought that I knew what I needed to know, but when I was asked to produce it, my information was scattered and incomplete. The problem wasn't that I hadn't studied enough. The problem was that I hadn't studied the right way.
Why do people make the same mistake that I did? Why do people who put so much effort into their education still fail to master what they set out to learn?
One of the core problems is that our built-in strategies and processes for self-study aren't calibrated to the actual requirements of learning. Familiarity and fluency are often conflated with mastery. Just because you recognize an answer doesn't mean that you know how to arrive at it. When we study, we confuse these two processes. It seems that we know things that we don't actually know.
I just memorized the information, why can't I recall it?
We have a tendency to confuse remembering with reading. When we study by reading over our notes, or rereading sections of the textbook, we experience the feeling of remembering. We recognize the information. But this isn't the same thing as recalling. It's only when we can recall the information from scratch that we can truly say that we know it.
Our tendency to confuse these two processes is natural. The act of remembering feels very similar to the act of reading. Our minds are always searching for meaning. So when we read something, we often feel the sensations of memory, even though we are just seeing them again for the first time.
But what is the difference between reading and remembering? And how can we fix our calibration?
One of the most important insights to come out of learning science in recent years was that we need to make our minds do the work. Our brains aren't passive instruments. We don't just write information down once and then have it for life. But if you think of your brain as a muscle, then you'll begin to see how we need to exercise it in order to strengthen it.
When we are studying, we need to engage in learning processes that require more work from our brains. And this needs to happen in a very specific way. We need to be producing the information that we are trying to learn. It's not enough to simply recall the information from memory. We need to produce it from scratch.
But how do we know if we are ready to produce information from scratch?
One powerful technique is called "self-generated recall". It's very simple: after you read a section from your notes or textbook, take a moment to quiz yourself on what you just read. The quiz doesn't need to be formal. You can simply ask yourself a few questions, such as "what was the main point from this section?" or "what was the conclusion from the last example problem?".
Testing yourself is the most powerful technique for building your confidence in your own learning.
It works because it shifts your focus away from reading and towards the more important activity of learning. When we are reading, we are focusing on meaning. But when we are trying to recall information, we need to focus on knowledge. We need to know what we know, not just understand what we read.
It works because it forces your brain to engage in more difficult processes. To recall something, your brain needs to do much more work than it needs to do to recognize the same information. And the more work your brain does, the more it will remember.
It works because it gives you honest feedback about what you know. We tend to convince ourselves that we know something that we don't. By forcing yourself to produce the information from scratch, you will see the gaps that are in your knowledge. By seeing these gaps early, you can begin to close them.
Self-generated recall is not the only technique that you should use to improve your learning. There are many other powerful techniques, such as spaced repetition and the spacing effect. But it is an important place to start.
If you want to learn more about other powerful learning techniques, sign up for my email newsletter
Where does this leave us?
The key to learning is to know what you know. We need to use our learning time effectively. To do this, we need to stop fooling ourselves that we know something that we don't. We need to stop thinking that effort equals progress. We need to stop thinking that familiarity and fluency are the same as mastery.
Mastery requires engagement. It requires fighting for learning. It requires engaging in difficult processes that cause the brain to do more work than it is used to. We need to know what we know.
The exam will come. We need to be prepared.
Until then, keep learning.

I felt like a car engine that had been revved high, only to be left without fuel. After the exam, I complained to a friend. "I just don't understand why I do so well in rehearsals, but freeze on the actual exam!" "Rehears and exams are different tests." My friend said. "In rehearsals, you are tested on what you know. In exams, you are tested on how well you are calibrated to produce under stress." "What do you mean?" "Think about it. When you prepare for an exam, you go over the material again and again. You learn the answers. But when you get to the exam room, you are not tested on your knowledge: you are tested on your ability to produce under pressure. You need to be calibrated for that."

In a 2013 meta-analysis, researcher Dunlosky found that the most widely used study strategies - rereading, highlighting, and summarizing - have very low utility. These techniques are good for familiarity with the material: you can recognize it and call it forth. But they are not good for recall, which is what exams are designed to test. Recognition is not the same as recall. If you can recite the multiplication table from memory, you might be able to produce 7*8 = 9*7 = 50. But it would be more difficult to get 7x8= 8x7 = 50, because you're trying to remember the answers in the right order, from scratch. If you've ever tried to read a novel in a foreign language, you know the difference between recognition and recall. You might be able to read the book in a single sitting, but understand almost nothing. Because you're only familiar with the words. You don't know their meaning. Familiarity is not mastery. And when you read something over and over again, you get more and more familiar with it. You can call it forth, and feel like you know it. But then when you get to the exam, you find that you can't produce it. And you go, "but I know this!" It feels very frustrating. But it's not what you know, but how you produce. And that's the calibration process: getting yourself calibrated to produce under pressure.

## Test yourself instead

The solution is to test yourself. Don't read the material over and over again. Don't highlight it, or summarize it. Use active recall. Test yourself. Spaced repetition will help you here. And you have to get honest feedback: did you get it right, or did you get it wrong? Without the feedback, you won't know how to fix it next time. We've implemented this in memrise through the mechanism of the "confused" and "got it" buttons. You press "confused" if you get it wrong, and "got it" if you get it right. Then the mem learning algorithm shows you the gap. If you press "confused", you might get a prompt: "what were the causes of WWI?" And if you got that right, you might get a prompt: "what were the causes of WWI in order:_____". But if you got that wrong, it will show you, "what were the causes of WWI in order? 1.____ 2. _____". And it shows it to you like that, with blank lines, because there's a gap in your understanding. And you can fill it in, because you have the feedback. And next time you get the prompt, you'll be able to fill it in faster and faster, and you will know that you've fixed the gap. And that's how you calibrate. The calibration process is not just about testing yourself. It's about getting honest feedback. About seeing the gap. About learning how to bridge the gap between familiarity and recall. And that's what the open-book exam was all about: showing the gap. Showing you where your mistakes were. Giving you the feedback.

## Predict, then compare

This approach of testing yourself to build calibration has been shown to be very effective in a study by Lovett and the Carnegie Mellon university. They showed that giving students a quiz at the start of the course and then comparing it with the final grade improved the final grade by 0.15 standard deviations. They also found that asking students to predict their own grade at the start improved the final grade by 0.13 standard deviations. And what they found was that the act of prediction, and then comparing that prediction with the final grade, had an enormous impact on the students. It made them feel like they had skin in the game. That their actions had consequences. That how well they did was important. And this meant that they were more careful about their studying, and more careful about getting the feedback that they needed to close the gap. So if you're studying for an exam, try this one question: what do you think your score will be? And then look at your score when it comes back. You might find that your score was lower than you thought. And you'll have learned something important: that your confidence can't be trusted. That's an important lesson to learn. And it's the lesson that matters, not the mark itself. Because you won't learn that lesson from the mark. You'll learn it from the gap. You'll learn it by comparing your understanding with what you got in the exam. And you'll learn it by getting honest feedback
